title: South Korea Approves How to Build a Nuclear-Powered Submarine. The Fuel Is Not in the Plan
dek: On Nov. 6 South Korea’s defense acquisition committee approved the basic strategy for Jang Bogo N: domestic development from 2027 and service after the late 2030s, with the cost still under analysis. The fuel those boats need depends on a U.S. agreement that has not been concluded and an IAEA arrangement Seoul has only begun to seek.

body_paragraphs.text: When South Korea’s Defense Project Promotion Committee met at the Ministry of National Defense on the afternoon of Nov. 6, the first item on its agenda was Jang Bogo N, the program to build the country’s first nuclear-powered submarines. The committee approved the program’s basic project strategy, according to the release the Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA) issued afterward and posted to the government’s Policy Briefing site on Nov. 9. On the submarine itself the release says little. It describes a domestic research-and-development program for a boat that can stay submerged longer and maneuver better than South Korea’s existing submarines, starts the work in 2027 and puts fielding sometime after the late 2030s. Where the total program cost would go, it says only that a cost analysis is under way.
Nearly everything else now reported about the decision came from a DAPA official at a background briefing the same day, as Yonhap News Agency relayed it.
The release itself does not mention the reactor, the fuel, the United States, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) or a shipbuilder.
Those omissions are, for the most part, the questions DAPA cannot settle on its own.

A basic project strategy fixes how a weapon will be acquired: developed at home or bought abroad, on what schedule and in what pieces. For Jang Bogo N, the briefing official said, the work will be split into four projects, all starting in 2027 — the submarine platform, development of the nuclear propulsion system, an integrated combat system and the supporting facilities.

The platform will be competed. DAPA plans to choose a builder through open bidding in the first half of 2027 and sign a contract by the end of that year, while the government procures the reactor directly rather than through the shipyard.
Some of the groundwork was laid earlier. In August, at DAPA’s request and on security grounds, the budget ministry exempted the program from a feasibility review, as it had the F-35A upgrade.

The schedule dates to May 26, when the Ministry of National Defense published its master plan for nuclear-powered submarine development, named the program and set out to launch the first boat in the mid-2030s and field it after the late 2030s.

What the strategy leaves open is the price and the size of the fleet. A detailed cost review is under way, DAPA officials told the Korea Times, and the price will be taken up with budget authorities early next year.
Media reports have put the program at three or more 8,000-ton boats and 28.9 trillion won (about $21.3 billion),
figures that appear nowhere in DAPA’s release.
Nor does the approval reach past the first effort: follow-on submarines will need decisions of their own.

Jang Bogo N is a program for nuclear propulsion, not nuclear arms. In the master plan South Korea states that it will neither possess nor develop nuclear weapons of any kind, and it commits the reactor to low-enriched uranium fuel, designed for long operation with as few refuelings as possible. The same document promises that Seoul will meet its nonproliferation obligations throughout the process of obtaining and managing that fuel, in close communication with the United States.

Washington’s part so far is a political approval. After President Lee Jae-myung’s meeting with President Donald Trump in 2025, the White House said the United States “has given approval for the ROK to build nuclear-powered attack submarines” and would work with Seoul on the project’s requirements, “including avenues to source fuel.”
The wording authorizes construction and promises help in finding fuel. It does not supply any.

For the fuel itself, DAPA officials have pointed to Section 91 of the U.S. Atomic Energy Act rather than a revision of South Korea’s civil nuclear cooperation agreement with Washington, citing AUKUS, the arrangement through which Australia is acquiring nuclear-powered submarines, as precedent.

Subsection 91c lets the President authorize the transfer of special nuclear material to an allied government for use in military reactors, on a presidential determination that it will promote the common defense and security — but only under an agreement for cooperation made under Section 123 of the same law.
Such an agreement must lie before Congress for 60 days of continuous session, referred to the foreign affairs and armed services committees of both chambers.
So far, one vice-ministerial round involving the foreign ministry has taken place, and no agreement exists.
Last week’s U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats won both chambers, appear in the Korea Times account as one of the program’s new hurdles.

The statute gives Congress a narrower lever than that suggests. A Section 91c agreement takes effect at the end of the review period unless a joint resolution of disapproval is adopted and enacted — legislation that a President who had negotiated the agreement could veto.

The harder dependency sits earlier, inside the executive branch: an agreement has to be negotiated and the President’s determination made before any review period begins, and after a single round of talks neither has happened.

The IAEA is the other outside party. Under Article 14 of a comprehensive safeguards agreement, a state that wants to use safeguarded nuclear material in a non-proscribed military activity, such as submarine propulsion, must first conclude an arrangement with the agency covering that material.

Seoul has opened that process without completing it. In June the agency’s director general welcomed South Korea’s intention to work with the IAEA on safety, security and safeguards measures for the submarines.

By September, he told the Board of Governors, South Korea had formally notified the Secretariat that it intended to begin consultations on an Article 14 arrangement and had already provided the relevant declarations.
Notice of intent to consult is the opening step. Neither statement describes terms, a draft text or a date.

Set side by side, the two tracks run at different speeds. The domestic one now has dates: a builder chosen in the first half of 2027, a platform contract by the end of that year and a first boat launched in the mid-2030s.
None of those steps needs fuel. The reactor does, and its development begins in 2027 as a separate project,
resting on a U.S. agreement and an IAEA arrangement for which the White House and IAEA statements give no timetable.
The next markers are concrete. Early in 2027 a cost figure is due to go to the budget authorities, and in the first half of the year DAPA’s competition for the platform should open.
On the other track, the signs would be a Section 91c agreement sent to Congress and a concluded Article 14 arrangement reported to the IAEA board.
Until those appear, South Korea has an approved way to build the submarine and no settled source for what will power it.

verification.locator: Report of 6 Nov 2026: DAPA official at a background briefing; builder via open bidding in H1 2027, contract by end-2027; government to procure the reactors directly; first launch mid-2030s, fielding after late 2030s; total budget not finalized; media reports of at least three 8,000-ton boats and 28.9 trillion won (US$21.3 billion). Its 'HALEU below 20 percent' phrasing is not used in the Brief.

Korean-language report of 6 Nov 2026 credited to Yonhap: four sub-projects (platform, nuclear propulsion system development, integrated combat system, facilities), all from 2027; platform competed, contract within 2027; feasibility study (사업타당성조사 as reported) waived in August by the Ministry of Planning and Budget at DAPA's request on security grounds, F-35A upgrade precedent; low-enriched uranium fuel. Not independent corroboration of s2.

Report of 8 Nov 2026: officials say fuel to be pursued through a separate arrangement under AEA Section 91, not by revising the 123 agreement, with AUKUS as precedent; one vice-ministerial consultation involving the foreign ministry held, no deal; Democrats won both chambers in the midterms; detailed cost review under way, price to be discussed with budget authorities early next year; strategy does not cover follow-on submarines.
